commentary_title: Surge in Panamax demand
commentary_summary: Drewry's tonnemile index for Panamax vessels stayed elevated after surging last month, with a 13% rise YoY. | This is juxtaposed with the lowest inactivity levels in the Panamax segment after the end of Covid lockdowns, resulting in ample supply in the market, squeezing utilisation levels. | The tonnage underway in the East has reached historically high. With more than 20 mdwt laden tonnage already waiting at the anchor at the discharge ports in the East, the congestion is likely to exacerbate in the region. | Despite ample coal trade in the Asian markets aiding vessel demand, the Baltic P5TC rates have been on a downward trend as vessel utilisation remained subdued.

commentary_title: Moderation in Drewry's tonnemile index
commentary_summary: Drewry's tonnemile index for Panamax vessels moderated for the second consecutive week but continues to be elevated YoY. | The tonnage underway in the East moderated last week from its historical peak but the share of laden tonnage in the region edged up. | Tonnage of approximately 7.5 mdwt is waiting at the anchor in the Pacific to unload cargo, the highest level attained in 2024 so far. The surge in US' grain exports to Japan and South Korea from the US West coast has been a significant contributor to the heightened activity in the region. | Additionally, the laden tonnage waiting at the anchor in China has reached its second-highest level in 2024 so far as coal and soybean imports remain buoyant.

commentary_title: Panamax utilization rises
commentary_summary: There was a slight increase in Panamax vessel utilisation, which rose marginally from 93.1% to 93.4% WoW. This 0.3% uptick is primarily due to robust activities in the coal market. | The heightened demand for coal in Asia, especially from China and India, driven by increased power consumption during the summer months, has significantly boosted coal imports. As a result, this seasonal surge in demand has led to a higher need for Panamax vessels, thereby boosting utilisation. | The laden tonnage at anchor in China has increased by 0.6 mdwt. This surge in congestion is attributed to substantial imports of soybean from Brazil and corn from Argentina. The influx of these agricultural commodities has resulted in a buildup of laden vessels at anchor, indicating heightened demand and seasonal peaks in import activities.

commentary_title: Surge in tonnemile index
commentary_summary: The Panamax vessel utilisation increased last week from 92.8% to 92.9%. However, the rise was marginal due to the contrary impact of change in laden and ballast speeds. While the global laden speed increased from 10.58 knots to 10.84 knots, the ballast speed dropped from 11.46 knots to 10.83 knots during the week, counterbalacing the impact on the vessel utilisation. | The tonne-mile index has risen significantly and reached its peak last week in 2024. The buoyant coal and grain trade continues to support Panamax demand, with the surge in the export of steel products aiding additional demand. | The tonnage underway in the East has been historically high in July 2024. With consistently strong coal trade between Indonesia and China, coupled with the surge in steel exports from China, Panamax demand in the region is high. The congestion at China's load ports reached the second-highest level in 2024 last week, indicating that exports from the region will rise in near-term.

commentary_title: Panamax utilisation rises
commentary_summary: There was a slight increase in Panamax vessel utilisation, which rose marginally from 91.6% to 92.0% WoW. This rise is attributed to the consecutively rising ballast speed, indicating positive sentiments in the market. | The tonnemile index reversed its downward trend last week and is likely to expand further with the growing soybean exports. | Simultaneously, the tonnage waiting at the load ports in the Atlantic has revived. However, it remains low YoY. However, due to the substantial decline in the laden tonnage at anchor in the Atlantic, the tonnage in port in the West has dropped to historically low levels.

commentary_title: Rise in Utilisation as speed increases
commentary_summary: The Panamax vessel utilisation expanded last week from 91.6% to 92.5%, after having declined for three consecutive weeks. This rise is attributed to consecutively rising ballast speeds, indicating positive market sentiment. | Meanwhile, the tonne-mile index rose sharply, reaching a higher level than last year, driven by buoyant soybean trade from ECSA, particularly Brazil. | Additionally, longer vessel routes due to Panama Canal congestion have boosted vessel demand of this segment. | As congestion at China's discharge ports has reached the lowest levels in 2024 so far, we project it to tread upwards in the upcoming weeks as China's soybean imports expand.

commentary_title: Stability in utilisation
commentary_summary: The global Panamax utilisation remained stable at 92.1% in week 41 and 42 of 2024, while continuing to be substantially lower YoY. | Meanwhile, the global tonne-mile index remained elevated as ample corn exports from the Atlantic have aided Panamax employability. US' corn exports have been on an uptrend despite lower imports from China. | Congestion at discharge ports declined in all major regions, except in the Indian subcontinent, where buoyant coal imports kept congestion high.

commentary_title: Surge in Panamax utilisation
commentary_summary: The utilisation of Panamax vessels rose from 91.4 % to 92.3 % last week but remained below the level in 2023. | Additionally, the tonne-mile index rose marginally, exceeding last year's level, driven by robust grain exports from the US Gulf and Brazil to Asia. | Meanwhile, the congestion increased in the Pacific due to high coal shipments from Australia and Indonesia.

commentary_title: Low seasonal demand impacts Panamax employability.
commentary_summary: The global Panamax utilisation witnessed a substantial fall, declining to 93.7% in the second week of 2025. | The Panamax tonne-miles index experienced a 2.6% WoW decline, reaching 96.8 points, attributable to seasonally low coal demand from Far East Asian market owing to Chinese new year holiday. | The tonnage waiting at the anchorage at China's discharge ports dropped to 3.4 mdwt, significantly lower compared to the same period in last two years. | The decline in tonnage underway in the east also corroborates the seasonal lull in China's markets.

commentary_title: Ballast speed improves, indicating gradual market recovery
commentary_summary: The global Panamax utilisation remained steady at 93.5% in week 6. However, the Panamax tonne-miles index declined 1% WoW, reaching 92.1. | Global laden speed increased by 2.5% WoW. Although global ballast speed is down YoY, it has increased marginally WoW and is in tandem with laden speed, indicating slow but gradual market recovery and increased vessel employment. | Increased days at anchorage for ballast vessels, in alignment with rising ballast tonnage at anchorage in the Pacific and Atlantic, will put pressure on vessel supply in the short term. However, it is not expected to impact rates in the immediately .

commentary_title: Panamax Tonne-miles index rises
commentary_summary: The Panamax Tonne-miles index increased 7 points over the week, reaching 103. The tonnage at the port and anchor declined MoM in the East with more vessels underway, pushing up the tonne-miles in the previous week. | The rise in tonnage underway supported the firming up of freight rates in week 11. Utilisation also increased marginally in tandem with the tonne-miles index. | Laden tonnage at anchor dampened WoW for China due to a decline in seaborne coking coal imports, attributed to increased overland imports from Mongolia. | Conversely, laden tonnage at anchor in India inched up WoW after two weeks of decline, due to the country's increased focus on domestic steel production which could potentially drive up coking coal demand.

commentary_title: Panamax utilisation dwindled
commentary_summary: The Panamax tonne-mile index experienced a 3% decline WoW in the second week of April. Concurrently, utilisation rates decreased by 0.3 percentage points, reaching 93.2%, leading to a softening of freight rates. | Spot rates on key routes saw significant drops, with the transatlantic and transpacific routes plunging by 18% and 23% WoW, respectively. A reduction in the percentage of laden tonnage in both eastern and western regions accompanied this decline. | Laden tonnage in India declined due to declining non-coking coal imports, which fell by almost 21% YoY in the past four weeks.

commentary_title: Panamax Index drops amid vessel speed changes
commentary_summary: The Panamax tonne-miles index declined by 4.4% in week 18 in tandem with falling ballast and laden speed. | Laden speed in the West dropped, accompanied by a decrease in the percentage of laden vessels in the region as vessels sought employment. | Vessels at anchor in the East increased 15.5% MoM, followed by increased congestion of both ballast and laden vessels in the East. | Laden tonnage in India increased due to increased thermal coal imports, which hit a 10-month high, led by a surge in shipments from Indonesia, resulting in improved market sentiments.

commentary_title: Panamax utilisation falls aas China cuts its coal imports
commentary_summary: The utilisation of vessels in the Panamax segment dropped to 92% in week 22, aligning with drop in the tonne-mile index. This moves in tandem with falling Baltic rates on major Panamax routes. | A key driver of this reduced utilisation is China’s decision to curb coal imports and encouraging power plants to stockpile domestically mined coal instead. This move comes amid falling domestic coal prices and an effort to support local miners after a significant output expansion. | However, increased Australian coal cargoes to India has contributed to growing congestion at Indian ports in week 22.

commentary_title: Panamax tonne-mile momentum accelerates due to robust soybean trade
commentary_summary: Panamax tonne-mile demand maintained positive momentum, rising 3.6% WoW in Week 26. This growth was primarily driven by stronger soybean shipments on the Brazil–China route. | Ballast tonnage in the Atlantic basin remained elevated, supported by the delayed soybean harvest in Brazil, which continued to fuel exports to China. Spot rates on this route rose by 9% in June, underlining robust demand. | Soybean exports from Argentina surged, doubling in June as suppliers rushed to ship cargoes ahead of the export tax hike scheduled for July. This further adds ballast tonnage to the Atlantic.

commentary_title: Panamax tonne-miles eases
commentary_summary: Panamax utilisation fell 1.2 percentage points in week 31 as the tonne- miles index weakened and Baltic rates softened; vessel capacity at anchor/port declined MoM as more vessels moved underway. | North Atlantic continued to ease due to muted demand and a lack of fresh inquiries, while South Atlantic stayed broadly steady after showing early signs of support that failed to sustain. | In contrast, the Pacific saw increased ballast congestion due to increased demand from Australia and Indonesia, followed by a new US–Indonesia trade deal reducing tariffs to 19% from 32%.

commentary_title: Panamax laden vessel queues surge at Chinese ports
commentary_summary: In late September, congestion worsened at China’s key dry bulk ports, Ningbo, Qingdao, Caofeidian and Rizhao, after Super Typhoon Ragasa disrupted transport links in the south. The storm delayed vessel arrivals and triggered ripple effects that spread congestion further north and east. | The disruption coincided with a surge in iron ore, coal and soybean shipments from Australia, Indonesia and Brazil. This influx of Panamax vessels placed significant pressure on berth availability, leaving many ships anchored offshore waiting for discharge slots. | While weather conditions have now improved, congestion remains heavy at Ningbo, Qingdao and Shanghai, where terminals are still managing high volumes of cargo. Backlogs are being addressed, but Panamax vessels carrying coal and grain are still facing prolonged waiting times | In the coming one to two weeks, waiting times are expected to ease as port operations normalise and capacity expands. However, continued strong flows of bulk shipments from Brazil and Indonesia mean queues are unlikely to clear completely in the short term.

Panamax tonne-mile index remained broadly stable in Week 43 | The Panamax tonne-mile index remained broadly stable in Week 43, as an increase in vessels waiting at anchor MoM in the West led to higher congestion, effectively tightening supply and supporting freight rates, reflected in the rise of the Baltic P5TC benchmark. | China’s suspension of US soybean imports amid trade tensions has disrupted seasonal shipping flows, with no cargoes arriving so far this season. Typically, 12 million tonnes move from the US to China between October and November, generating around 120 billion tonne-miles, roughly 12% of the total Panamax demand. The absence of this trade could remove 180–190 Panamax voyages leading to falling laden congestion in China. | At the same time, increased Indonesian and Australian coal shipments into India have added to laden congestion in the Indian Ocean, partially offsetting the demand loss. | Loading activity strengthened in the East and Indian Ocean, with the share of laden vessels rising to 60% and spot rates in the East spiking nearly 170% since the start of the year, reflecting robust regional demand.

commentary_title: Panamax market maintains firm momentum
commentary_summary: The Panamax market held a firmer feel overall this week with tonne-mile demand rose slightly 1.4% in week 47 to reach 109.3. In tandem, Benchamark baltic rates also followed this upward trajectory. | The USDA reported over 1.5 million tonnes of soybean sales to China last week, marking the first major purchase of the current marketing year, with shipments scheduled for two vessels, including a Kamsarmax. | Ballast congestion in the Atlantic is expected to edge higher in the coming weeks, supported by China stepping up US soybean buying and renewed demand from US Gulf grain and US East Coast coal trades.

commentary_title: Panamax Pacific market recovered after Indonesian coal weakness
commentary_summary: The Panamax market improved during the week, with the tonne-miles index reaching 114.8, an 11% YoY increase, and the Baltic benchmark P5TC rising to $19,825/day alongside increasing vessel Utilisation. The Atlantic remained the main driver, while Pacific gains were supported by improving demand from Australia and the North Pacific. | The Pacific started from a softer base as Indonesian round-voyage demand declined due to high coal inventories and weaker buying from end-user power plants. However, with a large number of spot vessels covered last week and fresh cargoes gradually returning, the market began to recover. Indonesia-South China rates improved, while tighter vessel availability in Australia supported overall sentiment. | The North Atlantic continued to strengthen as cargo demand outpaced available supply, particularly in the North Continent and the West Mediterranean. Transatlantic rates moved to over $21,700/day, while fronthaul and US East Coast- India business continued to firm. The South Atlantic also remained supported, with tight end-July tonnage.

commentary_title: Panamax utilisation remains high despite softer market indicators
commentary_summary: Panamax utilisation has eased from its 2026 peak but remains high. Utilisation reached a yearly high of 93.6% in week 26 before declining to 92.7% in week 30. Despite the recent easing, it remains above the 92.2% recorded in the same period last year. | Port congestion is becoming less supportive of the market, although conditions remain mixed by region. Laden congestion declined sharply in the East, China and Indian Ocean, while congestion increased in the Pacific, Oceania and Atlantic. Ballast congestion also declined in China and the Indian Ocean but increased in the Pacific and Atlantic. | Overall, easing congestion in key loading and discharge regions, combined with higher speeds, could continue to put pressure on utilisation if demand does not strengthen.

commentary_title: Stronger cargo flow drives the recovery in the Panamax market
commentary_summary: The Panamax utilisation rose to 93.2%, with improving market sentiment and stronger vessel fixing activity supporting gains in both the Atlantic and Pacific markets. The P5TC also firmed, closing the week at $20,834, as owners regained negotiating power following the tight vessel availability. | The Pacific saw the greatest improvement, with a smaller vessel availability and more cargo flow supporting higher rates. NoPac grain activity and Australian mineral demand pushed Kamsarmax rates high. Indonesian coal trades remained mixed, while the widening gap between C5–P3 spread could encourage additional Australian coal volumes to be loaded onto Panamax vessels. | Asian activity improved, supported by stronger Southeast Asian enquiries, giving owners greater confidence heading into September. The improving outlook was also reflected in increased activity during the period, with several vessels fixed for multi-month employment, signalling growing confidence in forward market conditions.

commentary_title: Atlantic market leads gains in the Panamax market as coal demand supports the Pacific
commentary_summary: The tonne-miles index rose 2.7 to reach 108.4 at the end of week 39, with tighter available tonnage and stronger cargo enquiry in the North Continent and West Mediterranean lifting Skaw-Gibraltar transatlantic route rates to $20,380/day. Fronthaul demand was even stronger. | East Coast Australia round-trip rates also increased, while Indonesian coal activity strengthened later in the week, with an 82,000-dwt fixing via Indonesia to India at $25,500/day. A relatively less tonnage list helps owners to maintain firm rates. | China’s August coal production fell 7% YoY, extending the contraction to 14 consecutive months, while coal-fired power generation has continued to outpace domestic coal supply. This widening supply-demand gap could support near-term coal imports and Panamax demand, although softer coal-fired generation may limit the upside.

commentary_title: Atlantic weakness weighs on Panamax rates
commentary_summary: Panamax rates softened over the week, with Atlantic demand remaining the main weakness, as limited fresh cargo enquiry weighed on transatlantic and fronthaul rates. | Congestion at both load and discharge ports has declined across most regions, except in the Indian Ocean. Lower congestion has released vessels back into the market, adding to available tonnage and putting pressure on charter rates. | The Pacific remains relatively better supported, with Australian cargoes and Asian coal demand providing employment, although this has not been sufficient to offset the weakness in the Atlantic.
